title: Variables
summary: Give a value a name, then use it.

steps.note: A variable is a name that holds a value. Start with a simple lowercase name.

choices.why: Correct. This name can refer to the text Mira.
A hyphen means subtraction in Python. Use an underscore or no separator.
A Python variable name cannot start with a number. Try a letter first.

steps.explain: The name on the left gives the value on the right a label.

steps.note: Use a variable's name without quotes to get the value stored inside it.

choices.why: Correct. Python looks up the value stored in name.
Quotes print the word name itself, not the value inside the variable.
Capital letters matter. The variable was created as lowercase name.

steps.explain: Without quotes, name refers to the value Mira.

steps.note: You can make another variable with a different name.

choices.why: Correct. This gives the place value its own clear name.
Quotes would make this text, not the name of a variable.
That would replace the value already stored in name.

steps.explain: A new variable name lets you keep a second value too.

steps.note: The variable name works anywhere a value is needed, including inside print().

choices.why: Correct. Python prints the value stored in city.
With quotes, Python prints the label city rather than its value.
The stored variable is lowercase city.

steps.explain: Using the variable name retrieves its current value.

steps.note: A variable can hold a number too. Do not put quotes around a number you want to keep numeric.

choices.why: Correct. This stores a number in age.
Quotes make 12 text instead of a number.
Python would look for another variable named twelve.

steps.explain: The number 12 is stored as a number because it has no quotes.

steps.note: Just like text values, numeric values can be printed by using their variable name.

choices.why: Correct. Python finds the number stored in age.
Quotes would display the word age instead of the number.
Python is case-sensitive, and the variable is lowercase age.

steps.explain: The variable name points to 12, so print() displays 12.
